news_drafts.headline: Denbighshire forecasts £5.2m overspend for 2026/27, with schools £5.4m over budget
news_drafts.lead:
Denbighshire County Council's Cabinet was told on 20 October that the council expects to end 2026/27 having spent £314.1m against a budget of £308.9m, a forecast overspend of £5.2m, or 1.7%. A forecast overspend is where a council expects to finish the year having spent more than it budgeted.

The schools budget, including the part of school funding the council does not pass directly to schools, is forecast at £103.9m against a budget of £98.5m. That is £5.4m, or 5.4%, over. It is the largest variance of any service in the budget summary, and it is larger than the overspend for the council as a whole.

The council's savings programme, the cuts and efficiencies it has committed to in order to balance its budget, set a target of £3.17m for 2026/27. The savings tracker shows £1.82m achieved, or 57.4%. A further £701k, 22.1%, is in progress. Proposals worth £648k, 20.4%, are marked "not achieved", and £738k of the target remains undelivered. The papers set out the figures but, in the extracts available, do not say how the council plans to close the gap.
news_drafts.paper_title: FINANCE REPORT - App 1 - Revenue Budget Summary

news_drafts.headline: Denbighshire revised corporate income forecast down by £28.2m to £1.1m and matched cuts to expenditure, keeping overall budget overspend at £510k
news_drafts.lead: Denbighshire Council has revised its corporate income forecast from £29.3m to £1.1m mid-year and made equivalent cuts to expenditure, leaving its net budget position unchanged. The £28.2m reduction in expected income — roughly nine-tenths of what was budgeted — has been matched by spending reductions of the same scale, keeping the council's overall budget overspend at £510k (0.2%) against a total budget of £309m. The adjustment reflects changed circumstances for income sources, though the council has not detailed which. Service-level overspends are modest: Adult Social Care and Homelessness, the largest service budget at £67.8m, is forecast to overspend by £442k; Planning, Public Protection and Countryside by £268k on a £12.2m budget. The overall position has deteriorated by £402k from the previous forecast.

findings.headline: Sole cashable benefit identified is licensing savings, "a small saving", realised after implementation and a transitionary period
findings.detail: The sole cashable benefit identified is savings on existing software licensing from moving to a hosted solution on mainstream technology. However, the amount is not quantified (described only as 'a small saving'), and these savings will only be realised after implementation and a transitionary period. The council must fund the full cost of both systems during transition before any offsetting benefit arrives.
findings.matters: A council is committing significant capital and revenue with only one financial benefit and that benefit is unquantified, described as small, and delayed, creating a prolonged period where the investment has no offsetting return to the budget.
findings.figures: Licensing savings described as 'a small saving'; timing post-implementation and transitionary period; amounts not specified
findings.quote: will allow us to make a small saving on licensing we currently have in place to cover the incumbent system's infrastructure

findings.headline: Implementation delay beyond August 2028 would trigger renegotiation of incumbent supplier contract at higher cost
findings.detail: The council's existing support contract for the current system (Open Housing) has a fixed extension deadline of 31 March 2028. The council targets decommissioning by 31 August 2028, creating a 5-month window. If this target is missed, the council would need to renegotiate a further extension with the supplier at terms the supplier proposes.
findings.matters: Project schedule slippage creates unbudgeted cost risk: missing the decommissioning deadline would force the council to renegotiate supplier contract terms at potentially significantly higher cost.
findings.figures: Current contract extension deadline 31 March 2028; decommissioning target 31 August 2028; 5-month contingency window
findings.quote: Should we not be able to decommission the system by 31/08/2028, we face having to reach an agreement to extend the support. It is likely that any further extension would see a potential significant increase in cost and may also require us to upgrade the system again.

findings.headline: Cost-benefit analysis incomplete and full project costs not disclosed in business case
findings.detail: The council's cost-benefit analysis is still under development and will be refined through several iterations. The business case references draft costs in Appendix 3 but this appendix is not included in the published version (marked as Part 2 confidential information). Full costs will only emerge when suppliers submit tender responses.
findings.matters: A council is advancing a major capital procurement without having completed its own cost-benefit analysis or disclosing project costs, raising questions about financial planning and decision-making.
findings.figures: Draft costs in Appendix 3 (not disclosed); full costs to be determined at tender evaluation stage; revenue costs for first 7-year term to be included in supplier pricing
findings.quote: The cost benefit analysis is still currently being developed. Given the uncertainty of the outcome of the procurement process, this is a complex process and will develop over several iterations of this Business Case.

findings.headline: Council committing to multi-year capital and revenue expenditure with no immediate cashable benefits
findings.detail: The council is committing to significant capital costs for implementation plus ongoing annual revenue costs for a replacement housing management system over a 7-year initial contract term, extendable annually. The business case explicitly states there are no immediate cashable benefits, with only non-cashable benefits and software licensing savings to be realised only after implementation and a transitionary period.
findings.matters: A council is making a major multi-year financial commitment with material revenue budget implications but no offsetting financial returns in the short to medium term.
findings.figures: Initial contract period 7 years with annual extension options to maximum 21 years; support contract for existing system expires 31 March 2027 with 12-month extension option to 31 March 2028
findings.quote: There are no immediate cashable benefits arising from the business case. However, following implementation and a transitionary period, savings on existing software licensing will be realised

findings.headline: Temporary borrowing from other councils reduced to £10m from £19m year-on-year
findings.detail: The council's reliance on short-term borrowing to manage cash flow decreased significantly during the year. This reduction of £9m represents a 47% decrease in temporary borrowing compared to the prior year end, suggesting improved cash flow management and reduced need for temporary funding solutions.
findings.matters: Reduction in short-term borrowing indicates improved liquidity and working capital management, reducing near-term refinancing risks.
findings.figures: Temporary borrowing £10m at 31 March 2026 vs £19m at 31 March 2025; reduction of £9m or 47.4%
findings.quote: At 31 March 2026 the Council had £10m in temporary loans from one local authority, compared to £19m at the previous year end 31 March 2025.
